title: Word families
lede: Learn one word and you've learned five. How word families work, why their spelling and sound shift, and how to use the right form every time.

sections.md:
## One root, a whole family
A **word family** is a base word plus every word built from it. Learn the family, not the word:

| Verb | Noun | Adjective | Adverb |
|---|---|---|---|
| decide | decision | decisive | decisively |
| persuade | persuasion | persuasive | persuasively |
| analyze | analysis | analytical | analytically |
| compete | competition | competitive | competitively |
| negotiate | negotiation | negotiable | — |
| economize | economy | economical, economic | economically |

This is the most efficient way to grow your vocabulary: every new base word brings three or four others with it.

## Two kinds of endings
Endings do two different jobs:

- **Inflectional endings** change *grammar* but not the word: *talk, talks, talked, talking*. Still the same word, still a verb.
- **Derivational endings** make a *new word*, often a different part of speech: *talk → talkative* (adjective). *Decide → decision* (noun).

Knowing which part of speech a sentence needs is the whole skill. "The judge made a final ___" needs a **noun** (decision). "She is very ___" needs an **adjective** (decisive).

sections.q: "Her ___ argument convinced the board." Which form fits?
sections.why: The blank describes *argument*, a noun, so it needs an **adjective**: persuasive.

sections.md:
## Families reveal hidden letters
Many English words have **silent letters** that are only silent in the short form. Add an ending and the letter wakes up:

| Silent | Spoken |
|---|---|
| si**g**n | si**g**nature, si**g**nal |
| mus**c**le | mus**c**ular |
| bom**b** | bom**b**ard |
| conde**mn** | conde**mn**ation |
| autu**mn** | autu**mn**al |
| solem**n** | solem**n**ity |

That's why the letter is there. English spelling often keeps a word family **looking** alike even when it doesn't **sound** alike. If you're unsure how to spell a word, say a relative out loud.

## Families reveal hidden vowels
The same trick fixes vowels you can't hear. In unstressed syllables, most vowels slur into an *uh* sound, so *definite* could be spelled -*ate*, -*ite*, or -*it*. Find a relative where that syllable is **stressed**:

- defin**i**te → def**i**nition (you hear the *i*)
- comp**e**tition → comp**e**te
- gramm**a**r → gramm**a**tical
- hum**a**n → hum**a**nity
- prepar**a**tion → prep**a**re

This one habit fixes hundreds of spelling mistakes.

sections.q: *Democrat* or *democrit*? Which relative lets you **hear** the vowel in the last syllable?
sections.why: In **demo-CRAT-ic**, that syllable is stressed, so the *a* is loud and clear. In *de-MOC-ra-cy* it's still slurred.

sections.md:
## Spelling changes inside families
Some families change spelling when they change form. These are the ones that trip people up:

| Base | Family member | Watch for |
|---|---|---|
| pronounce | pro**nun**ciation | the *o* disappears |
| explain | expl**an**ation | the *i* disappears |
| maintain | maint**en**ance | *-tain* becomes *-ten-* |
| proceed | proc**ed**ure | one *e*, not two |
| repeat | rep**et**ition | *-eat* becomes *-et-* |
| generous | gener**os**ity | the *u* disappears |
| curious | curi**os**ity | the *u* disappears |
| exclaim | excl**am**ation | the *i* disappears |

sections.title: Build a family
steps: Verb: **sustain** (keep going, hold up). Root **tain/ten** = hold; *sus-* = from below.
Noun: **sustenance** (*-tain* becomes *-ten-*, like maintain → maintenance) and **sustainability**.
sections.answer: **sustain, sustenance, sustainability, sustainable, sustainably.** One root, five words.

sections.md:
## Advanced: doublets
Sometimes **one Latin word** entered English **twice**, by two different routes, and became two different words. These are called **doublets**:

| Straight from Latin | Through French | Shared root |
|---|---|---|
| fragile | frail | *fragilis*, breakable |
| regal | royal | *regalis*, of a king |
| legal | loyal | *legalis*, of the law |
| hospital | hostel, hotel | *hospitale*, guest house |
| fact | feat | *factum*, a thing done |

The Latin-route word usually sounds more formal and technical; the French-route word sounds older and more everyday.

sections.label: Common traps
sections.md:
- **Economic vs economical.** *Economic* = about the economy ("economic growth"). *Economical* = saving money ("an economical truck").
- **Historic vs historical.** *Historic* = famous, important in history ("a historic win"). *Historical* = about the past ("historical records").
- **Continual vs continuous.** *Continual* = repeated with breaks ("continual complaints"). *Continuous* = with no break at all ("continuous noise").

sections.label: The habit that compounds
sections.md: Every time you learn a new word, write down its **whole family** in your notes. One new word a day is about 365 a year. One new *family* a day is well over 1,000.

practice.q: Fill in the right form of **decide**: "The judge's ___ was final."
practice.why: The blank follows *judge's*, so it needs a **noun**: decision.

practice.q: Fill in the right form of **maintain**: "Regular ___ prevents breakdowns."
Fill in the right form of **pronounce**: "Check the ___ before your presentation."
practice.why: **pronunciation**. The *o* drops out: pro-NUN-ciation, not pro-NOUN-ciation.
The blank describes *how she works*, a verb, so it needs an **adverb**: efficiently.
**Economical** = saving money. *Economic* means about the economy.

practice.q: Which word proves *competition* has an **e** in its second syllable?
practice.why: In **com-PETE**, the stressed syllable makes the *e* clear.

practice.q: Fill in the right form of **generous**: "Thank you for your ___."
practice.why: **generosity**. The *u* drops: generous → generOSity, like curious → curiosity.

practice.q: *Frail* and *fragile* both come from Latin *fragilis*. Word pairs like this are called…
practice.why: **Doublets**: one source word that entered English twice, by two routes. *Fragile* came straight from Latin; *frail* came through Old French.

practice.q: Using the doublet pattern, which is the French-route twin of **legal**?
practice.why: **Loyal**, from Old French *loial*. Both come from Latin *legalis*. *Loyal* first meant *lawful, honest*, and only later *faithful*.
practice.hint: Compare *regal* and *royal*. What happens to the *g* and the *e*?

practice.q: "The ___ of the old warehouse took two days." Which form of **demolish** fits?
practice.why: **Demolition**, from Latin *demolitio*. Like *abolish → abolition*, the -ish verb takes -ition. A rule this lesson didn't teach directly. Families have patterns you can extend.
practice.hint: What is the noun form of *abolish*?

practice.q: Which sentence uses the word correctly?
options: The museum keeps historic tax records from 1890.
It was a historic night: the first title in 40 years.
She wrote a historic report on 1890s tax law.
practice.why: **Historic** = important, famous in history: a first title in 40 years. **Historical** = from or about the past: tax records. The Alamo is *historic*.
practice.hint: One means *famous in history*; the other means *about the past*.
